=== FILE: videos/2020-03-13_kEjRVwJrzl0_the-sports-learning-curve-why-teams-are-slow-to-learn-and-ad/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: kEjRVwJrzl0
title: "SSAC20: The Sports Learning Curve: Why Teams Are Slow to Learn and Adapt"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Daryl Morey, Bill James, Sashi Brown, Richard Taylor (caption spelling), Kristen's Lee (caption spelling, student host)]
topics: [front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, american-football, basketball, other-sport:baseball]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel led by an economist asks whether teams in baseball, basketball and football learn from analytics, and how fast. The opening presentation takes two long-known mistakes per sport (bunts and steals, three-point shooting, fourth downs and draft pick valuation) and shows adoption was slow, in baseball taking decades. The panelists then offer reasons: a move that usually works feels right even when it is bad value, an organization needs understanding at every level, ownership must commit, and championships speed acceptance. The later discussion covers new frontiers (spatial football data, positionless basketball, two-way baseball players) and how to communicate with athletes. It matters as a set of first-hand explanations for why good analysis changes behavior slowly.

## Key claims

- The economist opens with the view that firms are assumed smart because competition would remove poor ones, and asks whether owners, managers and coaches count among the smart minority [02:04].
- Sacrifice bunts are poor value even when they succeed, since expected runs are about the same, and steals only add value above roughly a 75% success rate [03:07] [03:38].
- Bunt rates barely moved after an influential baseball publication in 1978, rose after a 2003 book, and fell only around 2011, when a movie came out [04:08] [04:39].
- Three-point attempts rose sharply without the success rate falling much [07:22] [07:54].
- Teams punt too much on fourth down; there has been some learning, with some regression last year [09:27] [09:59].
- The long-used draft pick chart reflects observed trade prices fit by hand, not the value of picks [11:33].
- By the presenters' estimate, the chart's top pick is worth five times the first pick of round two, but the second-round pick delivers more surplus; one could trade the top pick for five picks each worth more [13:05].
- Newer trades still follow the chart as a price list, and teams rarely trade unless paid the asking price [14:12] [14:44].
- Draft ranking carries little signal: the chance that a player ranked ahead of the next one is better is 52% overall, a bit higher in round one, and 52% again when re-estimated with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- One panelist says analysis can teach something different from playing; a move that works 60 to 70 percent of the time convinces people even when its failure cost is high, which kept the sacrifice bunt alive [16:52] [17:22].
- The same panelist says a general manager is limited by the decisions scouts and coaches make, so the whole organization must understand the approach, which takes a long time [17:55] [18:27].
- Another panelist says players, coaches, GMs and owners operate on different time cycles, and sustained change needs ownership buy-in and then a long turn [18:57] [19:29].
- He describes the coach of a high-scoring Phoenix team facing resistance from media and his own players, then trading for a traditional big man that hurt the team's play; he says that only a coach plus ownership buy-in plus visible success moves others [19:59] [21:32] [22:02].
- Another panelist says organizational commitment from ownership down is missing at most places, and that how information is presented matters as much as what it says [22:33] [23:03].
- A baseball panelist says a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM would shorten acceptance, but that the growing analytics community also shifts general culture [24:03] [24:33].
- The basketball panelist says every result becomes a referendum on a novel style, and more teams fail to win playing the traditional way than the new way [25:04] [25:34].
- A counterpoint is raised: the winning team had several of the best players in the league, so players may matter more than style, though teams copy what looks successful [26:04] [26:34].
- Copying superficial features fails, as with teams trying to rebuild a championship bullpen the next year; and power offense is said to work better in the postseason despite common belief [27:05] [27:35].
- The panelist who ran a football front office says he set out in 2016 to build draft capital and ended with almost two-and-a-half extra draft classes by selling into the pick chart's pricing [29:06] [29:36].
- A panelist says one team trades this year's picks for next year's, and that successors spent the accumulated picks quickly [30:37] [31:08] [31:41].
- Analytics must be integrated into decisions, not a separate group that enters and leaves the room [32:43] [33:14].
- Football information is new, and the football panelist says it has not yet been introduced in a compelling way; owners and executives need to align patience with plan timelines [33:44] [34:14] [34:45].
- The baseball historian (by context) says an analytically strong owner and four titles during his time at one club helped acceptance, while noting luck played a part [35:49] [36:19].
- The basketball panelist says being patient is very hard, as fans and friends react nightly, and it explains why organizations swing back and forth [37:19] [37:50].
- New frontiers named: football spatial analysis with tracking data, quarterbacks adapting college styles, fourth down, the draft, and pass defense [38:52] [39:23] [39:56].
- The economist notes pro football resisted going for it on fourth down while a football video game had to change its code to stop users from always doing so [40:58] [41:28].
- Opener pitching in baseball became real only around 2017 [41:28] [41:59].
- A panelist suggests playing the five best players regardless of position, noting that very skilled players are rarely also seven feet tall [43:02] [43:33].
- Baseball culture does not tolerate two-way players, and a successful exception comes from a different culture [44:34] [45:04].
- On a question about dehumanizing players, a panelist argues that treating them as commodities is what justifies large salaries [46:36] [47:08].
- The basketball panelist asks whether position-based estimates could blind teams to creative uses of players, and the historian says yes, which keeps analysts from becoming obsolete [48:12] [48:43].
- The football panelist says communicating with players and athletes is the new frontier [49:13]. The historian says one cannot convince athletes of anything without respect [51:50].
- Free-throw shooting and other skills are selected against other traits, and the open question is what can be taught [50:46] [51:17].
- The football panelist describes a high draft pick the staff believed they could teach to run routes, which did not work out within six or seven weeks; he says commitment needs humility about what can be changed [52:52] [53:22].
- Once baseball value is measured well, edge comes from finding improvable players, since all teams working from the same chart gives no edge [54:23] [54:54].
- The economist is not optimistic about teaching and says someone should write papers on what can be improved [55:58] [56:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Steal success needed to add value: about 75% [03:38]; in no year was league success 75%, though trending up [05:12] [05:47].
- Bunt and steal turning points: 1978 baseball publication, 2003 book, 2011 movie [04:08] [04:39].
- Lifetime three-point percentage .376 for one famous player on 1.9 attempts per game; another player with the same percentage takes 10 per game [06:19] [06:52]. The speaker also says .4 times 3 exceeds .5 times 2 [06:19].
- Pick chart: top pick said to be worth five times the first pick of round two [13:05]. Second overall asking price 2,600 points (caption: "twenty six hundred points") [14:12] [14:44].
- "Better than the next guy" statistic: probability that the player ranked n is better than n+1. 52% for the full draft, 56% for the first round (caption), and 52% again with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47]. Captions around "56%" are garbled.
- Four decades for baseball to learn [16:22].
- A move that works "51 percent" of the time with failure cost "three times" the payoff, versus 60 to 70 percent success [16:52] [17:22]. Captions are muddled here.
- Football front office goal: roughly a draft and a half of additional capital in two or three years; result almost two-and-a-half [29:36].
- Four World Series during one panelist's time with a club [36:19]. Opener pitching adopted around 2017 [41:59].

## Summary

A moderated football panel with an ESPN analyst, a team football operations executive and a college head coach. They discuss the pass-heavy offense moving into the NFL, why quarterbacks are hard to evaluate, what player tracking data can and cannot do, and how analytical information should reach coaches and players. The coach argues accuracy and elevating teammates are the key quarterback traits and are not coachable or measurable in simple ways. The analysts say tracking data helps with play classification and separating individual contributions, but decision-making remains hard to isolate. The sharpest disagreement is over fourth-down decisions and momentum. It matters as a plain view of where analytics and coaching judgment meet.
